bib.title: Language models for information retrieval (Chapter 12 of Introduction to Information Retrieval)
bib.venue: Cambridge University Press (online edition, draft April 1, 2009)

read.skipped: Nothing skipped; exercises 12.1-12.9 read but have no answers in the chapter.

question: How can a probabilistic language model of each document be used to rank documents for a query?
hypothesis: A document is a good match for a query if its language model is likely to generate the query, which happens when the document contains the query words often.
contributions: Introduces language models (12.1), the query likelihood model with smoothing (12.2), comparison with other IR approaches (12.3) and extensions: document likelihood, KL model comparison, translation models (12.4).

results.claim: Language modelling term weighting beats tf-idf on average 11-point precision in Ponte and Croft's experiments
results.setup: Ponte and Croft (1998): TREC topics 202-250 over TREC disks 2 and 3, sentence-length natural language queries; tf-idf is the INQUERY version with length-normalised tf; 11-point average precision; Wilcoxon signed rank test
results.note: Table prints +19.55 % change for the Ave row.
results.table: Figure 12.4, row Ave, columns tf-idf 0.1868, LM 0.2233, %chg +19.55

results.claim: Relative gain of LM over tf-idf is largest at high recall (+169.6 % at recall 0.8, 0.0160 to 0.0432)
results.setup: Ponte and Croft (1998): TREC topics 202-250 over TREC disks 2 and 3, sentence-length natural language queries; tf-idf is the INQUERY version with length-normalised tf; 11-point average precision; Wilcoxon signed rank test
results.note: Significant (*) only at recall 0.2 to 0.8 and Ave; the text says gains are at higher recall levels. At recall 0.9 the table prints +89.3 but 0.0063/0.0033 is about +91; likely rounding of unrounded inputs.

results.claim: At recall 0.0 the LM gain is small (+2.0 %, 0.7439 to 0.7590) and not significant
results.setup: Ponte and Croft (1998): TREC topics 202-250 over TREC disks 2 and 3, sentence-length natural language queries; tf-idf is the INQUERY version with length-normalised tf; 11-point average precision; Wilcoxon signed rank test

results.claim: Worked example 12.3: two-document collection with lambda = 1/2 ranks d1 above d2 for query 'revenue down' (3/256 vs 1/256)
results.setup: d1 and d2 each 8 tokens, collection 16 tokens; MLE unigram models mixed with lambda=1/2; query 'revenue down'
results.note: Arithmetic checked: correct. d2 lacks 'down' so gets only (0/8+1/16)/2 = 1/32 for it, which shows smoothing keeps its score non-zero.

results.claim: Example 12.1 prints P(frog said that toad likes frog) as about 1.573e-12, which matches five, not six, factors of 0.8
results.metric: P(frog said that toad likes frog)
results.setup: Unigram model of Fig 12.2 with STOP=0.2, continue=0.8, string of six words
results.note: INCONSISTENCY: the equation lists six 0.8 factors and one 0.2; 2.4e-11 × 0.8^6 × 0.2 = 1.258e-12, whereas 1.573e-12 = 2.4e-11 × 0.8^5 × 0.2. Recomputed by the extractor.

results.claim: Example 12.2 prints P(s|M1) as 0.00000000000048 (4.8e-13) but the listed factors multiply to 4.8e-15
results.setup: Seven-term sequence 'frog said that toad likes that dog' under M1 and M2 of Fig 12.3, STOP omitted
results.note: INCONSISTENCY: 0.01×0.03×0.04×0.01×0.02×0.04×0.005 = 4.8e-15, a factor 100 below the printed value. P(s|M2) = 3.84e-16 is printed correctly. The conclusion P(s|M1) > P(s|M2) holds either way; the true likelihood ratio is 12.5, not 1250.

results.claim: Printed P(s|M2) in Example 12.2 is correct at 3.84e-16

The book says LM retrieval has beaten tf-idf and BM25 weights, but doubts it is enough to justify replacing a well-tuned vector space system (quote: 'recent work has shown the LM approach to be very effective in retrieval experiments, beating tf-idf and BM25 weights'; 'perhaps still insufficient evidence that its performance so greatly exceeds that of a well-tuned traditional vector space retrieval system as to justify changing an existing implementation')
Smoothing is essential to LM retrieval, not only to avoid zero probabilities: it implements major parts of term weighting
results.setup: Query likelihood model with MLE unigram document models
results.quote: an unsmoothed model works badly because it lacks parts of the term weighting component

results.claim: Unsmoothed MLE gives conjunctive semantics: a document scores non-zero only if it contains all query terms
results.setup: Query likelihood with P(t|Md)=0 for missing terms
results.quote: then we get a strict conjunctive semantics

results.claim: Little smoothing suits short queries, much smoothing suits long queries; lambda can be a function of query size
results.setup: Linear interpolation or Bayesian smoothing; no numbers
results.quote: a small amount of smoothing (a “conjunctive-like” search) is more suitable for short queries, while a lot of smoothing is more suitable for long queries

results.claim: Mixing document and collection probabilities acts a little like idf
results.quote: terms rare in the general collection but common in some documents will have a greater inﬂuence on the ranking of documents

results.claim: Unigram models are used in IR because data per document is sparse (bias-variance trade-off) and they are cheaper (quote: 'Losses from data sparseness (see the discussion on page 260) tend to outweigh any gains from richer models')
results.setup: Document-level language models estimated from one document

results.claim: Lafferty and Zhai report model comparison (KL divergence) beats both query likelihood and document likelihood (quote: 'Lafferty and Zhai (2001) present results suggesting that a model comparison approach outperforms both query-likelihood and document-likelihood approaches')
results.setup: Risk minimisation framework, Fig 12.5; no figures given in the chapter

results.claim: Translation, relevance-feedback and model-comparison extensions each improve over basic query likelihood (quote: 'translation models, relevance feedback models, and model comparison approaches have all been demonstrated to improve performance over the basic query likelihood LM')
results.source: Berger and Lafferty 1999; Lavrenko and Croft 2001; Lafferty and Zhai 2001

results.claim: Smoothing a document LM with similar documents gives gains (Liu and Croft modest, Tao et al. larger)
results.source: Liu and Croft 2004; Tao et al. 2006
results.setup: Cluster-based and document-similarity smoothing; no numbers

limits: Only one empirical table (Fig 12.4, Ponte and Croft 1998, TREC 2 and 3 disks, topics 202-250); no results for smoothing methods, lambda values or BM25 comparison are given in the chapter.
Authors concede unigram models, no explicit relevance (hard to add relevance feedback or user preferences), and no phrase, passage or Boolean support.
Authors say the evidence is insufficient that LM beats a well-tuned vector space system by enough to justify switching.

Dated (2008): no neural or dense retrieval, no learned sparse models, no LLM generation; BM25 is the baseline, and Dirichlet-prior smoothing (Eq 12.11) is the form later used as query likelihood in toolkits.

Printed arithmetic errors in Examples 12.1 and 12.2 (see results notes). Eq 12.8 writes tf_{t,d} in the product over the vocabulary where the query count is meant. Eq 12.14 labels R as KL(Md||Mq) but the sum is over P(t|Mq) log P(t|Mq)/P(t|Md), which is KL(Mq||Md).
practices: Rank by P(q|Md) with P(d) uniform unless a genuine prior (authority, length, genre, newness, readership) is available (12.2.1).
Smooth document models with a collection model; do not use unsmoothed MLE (12.2.2).
Tune lambda or alpha by line search or EM; make it depend on query length: little smoothing for short queries, much for long (12.2.2).
Work with sums of log probabilities in practice (12.1.1).
Use multinomial rather than multivariate Bernoulli document models (12.2.3).
Use translation models to bridge synonymy or cross-language gaps, built from a thesaurus, bilingual dictionary or title/anchor-text pairs (12.4).
Two-stage smoothing (Bayesian then linear interpolation) is more stable than a single form (12.5, Zhai and Lafferty 2002).

terms.definition: a function that puts a probability measure over strings drawn from some vocabulary
throws away all conditioning context, and estimates each term independently
construct from each document d in the collection a language model Md and rank documents by P(q|Md)
P(t|d) = (tf_{t,d} + alpha P(t|Mc)) / (L_d + alpha); the collection model is a prior
probability of a query language model Mq generating the document
risk R(d;q) = KL between the document and query language models
generate query words not in a document by translation to alternate terms with similar meaning, P(q|Md) = prod_t sum_v P(v|Md) T(t|v)
